# Wasserstein GAN
The Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) is a modification of the standard Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to address training instability and gradient issues, particularly when the support of the generated distribution and the reference distribution are disjoint. In the standard GAN, the objective function relies on the log-likelihood ratio, which can result in vanishing gradients when the discriminator becomes too good, effectively stopping the generator's learning. WGAN resolves this by replacing the discriminator with a "critic" function constrained by a bounded Lipschitz norm, ensuring stable gradients. This constraint is enforced through techniques such as weight clipping, spectral normalization, or gradient penalty.
By utilizing the Kantorovich-Rubenstein duality theorem, WGAN reformulates the game's objective to minimize the 1-Wasserstein distance between the generated distribution and the reference distribution. This distance metric provides a meaningful measure of "far-ness" even when the distributions do not overlap, allowing the generator to receive consistent learning signals. Consequently, WGAN avoids the mode collapse often seen in standard GANs and achieves more stable convergence during training.
